task1.title: Forest industry products
task1.prompt: The graph below shows the production of three forest industry products in a European country, namely timber, pulp, and paper, from 1980 to 2000.

chartDesc.title: Forest industry production, 1980-2000
chartDesc.overview: Paper production experienced the strongest growth overall, eventually surpassing both timber and pulp to become the highest produced item by 2000. Timber production peaked mid-period before declining, while pulp dipped sharply early on before steadily climbing.
keyFeatures: Paper production increased steadily from the lowest start of 4 million tonnes in 1980 to reach the highest overall total of 12 million tonnes in 2000.
Timber peaked in 1985 at 10 million tonnes, making it the dominant product at that time, before dropping to 7.5 million tonnes by 2000.
Pulp dropped sharply between 1980 and 1983 to around 2.5 million tonnes before recovering to nearly 10 million tonnes by 2000.

task1.instruction: Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparison where relevant.
task1.sampleBand5:
The graph shows the production of timber, pulp and paper in a country in Europe between 1980 and 2000.

Overall, the production of paper increased, and timber production also increased but then it went down. The pulp production stayed about the same.

In 1980, the production of timber was about 8 million tonnes. Then it went up to about 10 million tonnes in 1990. After that it decreased a lot to about 6 million tonnes in 2000. The pulp production was about 6 million tonnes in 1980 and it was still about the same in 2000. The paper production started at about 4 million tonnes in 1980. After that it increased to about 8 million tonnes in 2000. So, paper production had the biggest increase. The pulp production didn't change very much during this time.

Overall, timber production experienced a general increase, while pulp and paper production fluctuated. There were some periods of growth and decline for all three products.

In 1980, timber production started at around 4 million tonnes. It then increased steadily to reach a peak of about 8 million tonnes in 2000. Pulp production began at approximately 10 million tonnes, and it increased to around 12 million tonnes in 1990. After that, it decreased to some extent to finish at just below 12 million tonnes in 2000. Paper production started at about 6 million tonnes in 1980. It went up to around 8 million tonnes in 1990, before falling back to 6 million tonnes in 2000. The production levels were quite similar at the start and end for paper.

It is clear that timber had the most significant increase, while paper and pulp production stayed relatively stable.

The line graph depicts the fluctuating production levels of timber, pulp, and paper in a certain European country over a twenty-year period, from 1980 to 2000.

An initial overview reveals that paper production experienced the most significant growth, while timber production saw a period of decline before recovering. Pulp production, conversely, remained relatively stable throughout the period, albeit with some minor oscillations.

In 1980, timber production stood at approximately 12 million tonnes, but this witnessed a steady downturn to reach a low of around 8 million tonnes by 1990. Subsequently, it underwent a resurgence, climbing back to approximately 12 million tonnes by the year 2000. Starting at around 6 million tonnes in 1980, it increased steadily, surpassing timber production in the mid-1990s and ultimately reaching a peak of approximately 16 million tonnes by 2000. task1.sampleAnswer:
The line graph illustrates the production levels of three forest industry products—timber, pulp, and paper—in a European country over a twenty-year period from 1980 to 2000. Overall, while paper production increased significantly, timber and pulp showed more variable trends over the period.

In 1980, timber production was the highest among the three products at approximately 35 million tonnes, followed by pulp at around 25 million tonnes and paper at roughly 20 million tonnes. Over the following decade, timber production fluctuated, dipping to about 30 million tonnes in 1985 before recovering to 35 million tonnes by 1990.

Paper production showed the most consistent growth, rising steadily from 20 million tonnes in 1980 to approximately 40 million tonnes by 2000, eventually surpassing timber as the dominant product. Pulp production remained relatively stable throughout the period, hovering around 25-30 million tonnes.

By 2000, paper had become the leading product, with timber in second place at around 32 million tonnes and pulp remaining the least produced at approximately 28 million tonnes. The most notable trend was the reversal in the positions of paper and timber.

task2.title: Schools teaching good behaviour
task2.prompt: It is the responsibility of schools to teach children good behaviour in addition to providing formal education. To what extent to you agree or disagree?
task2.instruction: To what extent to you agree or disagree?
task2.sampleBand5:
Schools are very important. They teach children many things like reading and writing. But some people think schools should also teach children how to behave well. I agree with this to some extent.

It is important for children to learn good behaviour. If they don't, they might be rude to other people. They might not listen to their teachers. This can make problems in the classroom. If schools teach good behaviour, children will know how to treat others with respect. They will also learn how to follow rules.

Parents also have a role to play. They should teach their children good manners at home. But sometimes parents are busy. They don't have time to teach their children everything. So schools can help. Schools have teachers who are trained to teach children. They can teach children about sharing and being kind.

However, schools should not only focus on behaviour. They also need to teach academic subjects. Children need to learn maths, science, and history. These subjects are important for their future. If schools only teach behaviour, children might not get a good education. This is not very good.

In conclusion, I think schools should teach children good behaviour. But they should also teach academic subjects. Both are important for children's development. Schools can help parents, but parents also have a responsibility. It's important to find a balance.
task2.sampleBand6:
It is often said that schools should not only provide education but also teach students how to behave well. I somewhat agree with this statement. While parents have a primary role in shaping a child's character, schools also have an important part to play.

On the one hand, the family is where children first learn about values and ethics. Parents are the first role models, and they teach their children the difference between right and wrong. It is also true that different families have different ideas about what good behaviour actually is. Therefore, it is difficult for schools to impose a single standard that everyone agrees with.

However, schools are a place where children spend a lot of time, and they interact with many other people. Schools can teach students important social skills like how to cooperate, how to respect others, and how to resolve conflicts peacefully. Furthermore, schools can provide a structured environment where good behaviour is rewarded and bad behaviour is punished. This can help children learn to make good choices.

Of course, schools should not try to replace parents. The best approach is for schools and families to work together to teach children good behaviour. Parents can reinforce the lessons that children learn at school, and schools can support the values that children learn at home. In addition, schools can teach children about citizenship and their responsibilities to the community.

In conclusion, while parents have the main responsibility for teaching their children how to behave, schools also have a significant role to play. By working together, families and schools can help children grow into responsible and well-behaved adults. I believe it is important for schools to actively promote good behaviour among their students.
task2.sampleBand7:
The issue of whether schools should be responsible for teaching children good behaviour, in addition to providing formal education, is a subject of much debate. While some argue that this is primarily the role of parents, I believe that schools have a significant, and perhaps even vital, role to play in shaping a child's character and instilling positive values. To a considerable extent, the responsibility should be shared between home and school.

One of the main reasons why schools should be involved in teaching good behaviour is that children spend a significant portion of their time at school. During these formative years, they are constantly observing and learning from their teachers and peers. Consequently, the school environment can have a profound impact on their developing sense of right and wrong. If schools actively promote values such as respect, empathy, and responsibility, children are more likely to internalise these values and demonstrate them in their interactions with others. For example, implementing programs that encourage teamwork and conflict resolution can help children develop crucial social skills and learn how to behave appropriately in different situations.

Furthermore, not all children receive adequate guidance on behaviour at home. Some parents may be too busy to dedicate sufficient time to teaching their children proper manners and social etiquette. In other cases, parents may lack the necessary skills or knowledge to effectively guide their children's behaviour. In such situations, the school can act as a crucial support system, providing children with the guidance and structure they need to develop into well-rounded individuals. This is not to say that schools should replace parents, but rather that they should supplement the efforts of parents and provide additional support where needed.

However, it is important to acknowledge that the primary responsibility for teaching children good behaviour ultimately lies with parents. Parents are the first role models in a child's life, and they have the greatest influence on their children's values and beliefs. Schools can reinforce the values that are taught at home, but they cannot completely compensate for a lack of parental involvement. It is therefore essential that parents and schools work together to create a consistent and supportive environment for children to learn and grow.

In conclusion, while parents undoubtedly play a crucial role in teaching children good behaviour, schools also have a significant responsibility in this area. By actively promoting positive values and providing guidance and support, schools can help children develop into responsible and well-behaved members of society. This collaborative approach, where both parents and schools work together, is the most effective way to ensure that children receive the comprehensive education they need to thrive.
task2.sampleBand8:
The question of whether schools should be responsible for teaching children good behaviour, in addition to providing formal education, is a complex one. While the primary function of schools is undoubtedly academic instruction, I strongly believe that instilling positive character traits and ethical conduct is an equally vital, complementary role that schools must embrace.

Firstly, the family unit, traditionally considered the primary source of moral guidance, is increasingly facing challenges in the modern world. With both parents often working long hours, and the prevalence of single-parent households, children may not always receive the consistent and comprehensive guidance they need to develop into responsible and well-behaved individuals. Therefore, schools can effectively supplement the efforts of parents by explicitly teaching values such as respect, empathy, and honesty. For instance, implementing programmes that promote conflict resolution skills or encourage community service can have a profound impact on students' behaviour, both within and outside the school environment. Many schools now incorporate restorative justice practices, which help students understand the impact of their actions and take responsibility for them, fostering a sense of accountability.

Secondly, schools provide a unique social environment where children interact with peers from diverse backgrounds. This setting presents valuable opportunities to learn essential social skills, such as cooperation, teamwork, and tolerance. By creating a supportive and inclusive school culture, educators can actively model and reinforce positive behaviours. Moreover, teachers can serve as role models, demonstrating ethical conduct and exemplifying respectful communication. Furthermore, schools are uniquely positioned to address issues such as bullying and cyberbullying, which are prevalent in today's society. Educating students about the harmful effects of these behaviours and providing them with strategies to prevent and respond to them is crucial for creating a safe and respectful learning environment. To illustrate, anti-bullying workshops and peer mentoring programs can be invaluable tools in promoting positive social interactions and preventing harmful behaviours.

In conclusion, while academic excellence remains a core objective of education, it is equally important for schools to actively contribute to the development of well-rounded individuals with strong moral character. By integrating character education into the curriculum and fostering a positive school culture, schools can play a crucial role in shaping the next generation of responsible and ethical citizens. This holistic approach to education, which encompasses both academic and behavioural development, is essential for preparing children to thrive in an increasingly complex and interconnected world. It is therefore my firm conviction that schools have a significant responsibility to teach children good behaviour, alongside formal education.
task2.sampleBand9:
The debate surrounding the role of schools in shaping children's behaviour, beyond their academic instruction, is a complex one. While formal education undeniably holds paramount importance, I strongly believe that schools also bear a significant responsibility in nurturing positive behavioural traits in students, as these qualities are intrinsically linked to their overall development and future success.

Firstly, schools represent a microcosm of society. Children spend a considerable portion of their formative years within the school environment, interacting with peers and teachers from diverse backgrounds. This setting provides an ideal platform for learning and internalizing crucial social skills such as empathy, respect, and cooperation. By actively promoting and modelling good behaviour, schools can equip students with the interpersonal skills necessary to navigate social complexities and contribute positively to their communities. Neglecting this aspect of education would be a disservice to students, potentially hindering their ability to form healthy relationships and function effectively in collaborative settings.

Secondly, instilling good behaviour can directly enhance academic performance. A classroom environment characterized by discipline and mutual respect fosters a conducive atmosphere for learning. When students are taught to listen attentively, participate constructively, and resolve conflicts peacefully, teachers can dedicate more time to instruction and less time to managing disruptive behaviour. Moreover, qualities such as diligence, perseverance, and a strong work ethic, which are integral components of good behaviour, are also essential for academic achievement. Therefore, by actively cultivating these traits, schools can indirectly but significantly improve students' academic outcomes.

Admittedly, the primary responsibility for shaping a child's behaviour lies with their parents or guardians. However, the influence of the school environment should not be underestimated. In many cases, schools serve as a vital support system, particularly for children from disadvantaged backgrounds where positive role models may be lacking. Furthermore, schools can reinforce the values and principles taught at home, creating a synergistic effect that strengthens a child's moral compass. Ultimately, a collaborative effort between parents and schools is crucial for holistic child development.

In conclusion, while formal education remains the core function of schools, their role in teaching good behaviour is equally important. By fostering a positive and supportive learning environment, schools can equip students with the social and emotional skills necessary to thrive both academically and personally. Therefore, I firmly believe that schools have a moral imperative to prioritize the development of well-rounded individuals who are not only knowledgeable but also responsible and compassionate citizens. The confluence of academic excellence and exemplary behaviour should be the hallmark of a comprehensive education.
task2.sampleAnswer:
There is an ongoing debate about whether schools should bear responsibility for teaching children good behavior alongside academic subjects. I strongly agree that schools play a vital role in shaping students' conduct and values, and this should be considered an integral part of their educational mission.

Firstly, children spend a significant portion of their formative years in school, making it one of the most influential environments in their lives. Schools provide a structured social setting where children interact with peers and authority figures, offering countless opportunities to learn appropriate behavior. Through classroom rules, group activities, and interactions with teachers, students can develop essential social skills such as respect, cooperation, and conflict resolution.

Secondly, not all children receive adequate behavioral guidance at home. Some parents may lack the time, resources, or skills to instill good values in their children. In such cases, schools can serve as an equalizing force, ensuring that all children, regardless of their home situation, are exposed to positive behavioral models and expectations. Teaching good behavior at school can help compensate for gaps in parental guidance.

However, it is important to acknowledge that schools cannot solely be responsible for children's behavior. Parents remain the primary role models and must reinforce at home the values taught at school. A collaborative approach between schools and families would be most effective.

In conclusion, I firmly believe that teaching good behavior should be considered a core responsibility of schools, working in partnership with parents to develop well-rounded, socially responsible individuals.

Maktablar juda muhim. Ular bolalarga o'qish va yozish kabi ko'p narsalarni o'rgatadi. Ammo ba'zi odamlar maktablar bolalarga o'zini yaxshi tutishni ham o'rgatishi kerak deb o'ylashadi. Men bunga ma'lum darajada qo'shilaman.

Bolalarga yaxshi xulq-atvorni o'rganish muhim. Agar ular o'rganmasa, boshqa odamlarga qo'pol munosabatda bo'lishi mumkin. Ular o'qituvchilarini tinglamasligi mumkin. Bu muammolarni keltirib chiqarishi mumkin sinfda. Agar maktablar yaxshi xulq-atvorni o'rgatsa, bolalar boshqalarga hurmat bilan munosabatda bo'lishni bilishadi. Ular, shuningdek, qoidalarga rioya qilishni o'rganadilar.

Ota-onalar ham o'z rolini o'ynashi kerak. Ular farzandlariga uyda yaxshi odob-axloqni o'rgatishlari kerak. Ammo ba'zida ota-onalar band bo'lishadi. Ularning farzandlariga hamma narsani o'rgatishga vaqti yo'q. Shunday qilib, maktablar yordam berishi mumkin. Maktablarda bolalarga ta'lim berish uchun tayyorlangan o'qituvchilar bor. Ular bolalarga baham ko'rish va mehribon bo'lish haqida o'rgatishi mumkin.

Biroq, maktablar faqat xulq-atvorga e'tibor qaratmasligi kerak. Ular, shuningdek, akademik fanlarni o'qitishlari kerak. Bolalar matematika, fizika va tarixni o'rganishlari kerak. Bu fanlar ularning kelajagi uchun muhim. Agar maktablar faqat xulq-atvorni o'rgatsa, bolalar yaxshi ta'lim olmasligi mumkin. Bu juda yaxshi emas.

Xulosa qilib aytganda, menimcha, maktablar bolalarga yaxshi xulq-atvorni o'rgatishi kerak. Ammo ular, shuningdek, akademik fanlarni o'qitishlari kerak. Ikkalasi ham bolalarning rivojlanishi uchun muhim. Maktablar ota-onalarga yordam berishi mumkin, lekin ota-onalarning ham mas'uliyati bor. Muvozanatni topish muhim.
task2.uzSampleBand6:
Ko'pincha maktablar nafaqat ta'lim berishi, balki o'quvchilarga o'zini yaxshi tutishni ham o'rgatishi kerakligi aytiladi. Men bu fikrga qisman qo'shilaman. Bolaning xarakterini shakllantirishda ota-onalarning asosiy roli bo'lsa-da, maktablar ham muhim rol o'ynaydi.

Bir tomondan, oila - bu bolalar qadriyatlar va axloq haqida birinchi bo'lib o'rganadigan joy. Ota-onalar birinchi namuna bo'ladi va ular bolalariga yaxshi va yomon o'rtasidagi farqni o'rgatadi. Shuningdek, shuni ham aytish kerakki, turli oilalar yaxshi xulq-atvor nima ekanligi haqida turli xil tasavvurlarga ega. Shuning uchun maktablar hamma rozi bo'ladigan yagona standartni o'rnatishi qiyin.

Biroq, maktablar - bu bolalar ko'p vaqt o'tkazadigan va boshqa ko'plab odamlar bilan muloqot qiladigan joy. Maktablar o'quvchilarga hamkorlik qilish, boshqalarni hurmat qilish va nizolarni tinch yo'l bilan hal qilish kabi muhim ijtimoiy ko'nikmalarni o'rgatishi mumkin.
